Spawned backend design study

Measured runtime, transport, scheduler and I/O experiments. Read the methodology and compatibility limits before choosing a backend. Public actor/protocol APIs and production defaults are unchanged.

How to read this report

Each platform is analyzed separately. Linux is an OrbStack ARM64 VM/container, not bare metal. Lines and bars use medians; error bars show observed min/max across repeated processes, not confidence intervals. Failed starts and watchdogs are retained and excluded from performance medians. Prototype controls omit some actor lifecycle semantics, so raw speed alone is not a replacement criterion.

1,134 measured processes; 1,125 completed; 113,200,977 validated requests/echoes. Raw datasets and hashes.

Findings and decision

Keep Tokio as the default. Continue sharded and adaptive runnable scheduling as opt-in research candidates, and improve dedicated-runtime resource ownership separately. This campaign finds useful design tradeoffs, not a universal replacement. Native scheduler controls do not yet implement Spawned's full lifecycle or async handlers. Three short repetitions on an unpinned host are descriptive evidence, not a statistical proof or a production capacity forecast.

What we learned on macOS

1,024 actors / 256 producers Median replies/s Median completion p99 Runtime/scheduler workers
Spawned async 459,298 0.850 ms 2
Native ready queue, adaptive batch 545,723 0.560 ms 2
Native ready queue, fixed batch 16 462,953 0.645 ms 2
Spawned synchronous thread actors 276,040 0.730 ms 1 thread per actor
Spawned async 545,484 1.444 ms 16
Native ready queue, adaptive batch 515,021 0.472 ms 16

The adaptive control's two-worker median is 18.8% above async, but their observed throughput ranges overlap: async 458,895–561,504 and adaptive 493,039–571,128 replies/s. With sixteen workers async leads median throughput. Every row still has producer/observer threads outside the scheduler worker count. Native controls use bounded concrete messages; the framework uses boxed envelopes and has more semantics. This does not isolate batching as the cause of the entire difference.

Other concrete findings:

  • Spinning buys latency with reserved CPU. Four idle native-spin actors use about 3.94 process CPU seconds per wall second. Blocking and short-spin controls round to approximately zero at the process timer's resolution. This is not a wattage measurement. Continuous spinning belongs only in a deliberately provisioned low-latency mode, if later application tests justify it.
  • Per-actor reactors have a resource ceiling. dedicated-current at 1,024 actors failed all three starts with the host's 4,096-descriptor soft limit. Raising only the benchmark child's limit to 16,384 let all three runs complete (median 261,070 replies/s). Removing helper runtime threads does not eliminate per-actor reactor costs.
  • Persistent blocking-pool actors can exhaust their executor. At 1,024 actors, all three Backend::Blocking samples hit the 15-second watchdog; at 512 actors all three completed. Linux reproduced the same three watchdogs at 1,024 actors and three completions at 512. The benchmark's Tokio builder leaves the blocking-pool maximum at its dependency's default of 512, and each actor retains a blocking worker for its loop. The stalled warmup is consistent with queued actor loops having no worker available. This is a capacity/liveness result, not zero measured throughput.
  • A shared helper runtime is a tradeoff, not a free win. The process-managed two-worker variant reaches only about 60k replies/s at 1,024 actors on this host. The separate caller-owned shared variant additionally depends on caller runtime lifetime. Current-thread mode cannot progress a spawned helper while its owner thread blocks. All are characterized explicitly by compatibility tests.
  • Reply shape matters. In matched async Probe tests, Tokio oneshots use about 3 allocation/reallocation calls per request versus about 6 for either standard channel. The normal async request path already uses Tokio oneshots: this is evidence against replacing them casually, not a newly discovered optimization of that path. Counts include driver activity.
  • A bounded queue can make a burst latency chart misleading. A 256-slot queue blocks producers, delaying subsequent request timestamps. When capacity is raised to 131,072 in the control, native burst completion p99s grow into roughly 91–183 ms. Their earlier few-millisecond tails were partly admission behavior, not an equivalent offered workload being processed dramatically faster.
  • Static placement needs skew tests. In the two-worker hotspot case, sharded-16 cold-actor p99 is 2.912 ms, versus 0.726 ms for async and 0.216 ms for ready-adaptive. This includes placement imbalance; it does not establish a general scheduling or fairness ranking.
  • I/O architecture matters as much as the API. In the supplemental 128-socket macOS test, one-reactor Monoio kqueue and Tokio reach similar median throughput (239k and 236k echoes/s), with different tails (0.724 and 2.974 ms). Four client reactors yield about 210k and 198k/s; Tokio's tail improves to 0.843 ms. More reactors do not automatically improve throughput. The common echo server still uses one thread per socket, and this is loopback I/O rather than a networked application benchmark.

What we learned in the Linux VM

The container has four allowed CPUs, 8 GiB RAM and a 4,096-PID limit. Its main scheduler matrix uses two workers, with a separate four-worker control. The main subset covers ten implementations and seven message cases plus all ten I/O controls; macOS covers the wider message matrix. Neither CPU affinity per worker nor bare-metal Linux was tested. Compare rows within each environment.

1,024 actors / 256 producers Median replies/s Median completion p99 Workers
Spawned async 942,293 0.696 ms 2
Global ready queue, adaptive 748,750 0.464 ms 2
Local ready queues, batch 16 964,785 0.472 ms 2
Scanning shards, batch 16 1,212,820 0.413 ms 2
Spawned async 1,081,213 2.150 ms 4
Global ready queue, adaptive 883,769 0.424 ms 4
Local ready queues, batch 16 1,254,441 0.449 ms 4
Scanning shards, batch 16 1,266,961 0.514 ms 4

The global adaptive scheduler's macOS advantage does not reproduce here. Sharding is the more promising large-population Linux control. However, at 128 actors with four workers, async reaches 2.55M replies/s versus 2.50M for scanning shards and 1.60M for local ready queues. There is no single scheduler winner across scale, worker budget and platform. These remain concrete-message controls with fewer semantics than Spawned.

For 128 persistent loopback sockets with four client reactors:

Client mechanism Median echoes/s Median echo p99
Tokio / epoll 992,365 0.825 ms
Monoio / epoll 1,285,613 0.700 ms
Monoio / io_uring 862,842 0.307 ms

Explicit io_uring worked without fallback. It improves the measured tail versus both four-reactor readiness controls, but does not lead throughput. The Monoio epoll throughput range is wide (1.15M–1.86M/s); three processes do not establish a stable production advantage. With one reactor, Monoio epoll and io_uring reach about 502k and 468k/s. Buffer ownership, executor behavior, syscall choices and reactor parallelism all change between controls. This does not measure the isolated effect of io_uring or justify replacing Tokio.

What should become library work

  1. Preserve the current actor/protocol APIs and Tokio default while improving measurements and runtime guidance. Document blocking-pool saturation and dedicated-runtime ownership explicitly.
  2. Evaluate sharded ownership and bounded turns/adaptive batching in a backend that actually runs Spawned envelopes, async handlers, cancellation, monitors and panic cleanup. Compare it with the existing executor at the same worker budget; do not ship the benchmark loop as a finished backend.
  3. Investigate an explicitly owned shared runtime for dedicated actors, with helper-task isolation, shutdown and lifetime contracts. The current managed prototype's poor large-population result rules out promoting it unchanged.
  4. Treat thread/core affinity, short spinning and sharded placement as optional specialist policies. Add work-stealing/placement experiments before selecting a static layout for uneven traffic. No affinity or work-stealing backend was measured here.
  5. Consider a Linux io_uring or portable non-Tokio backend only after bridging the current Send handler model, timers and application I/O compatibility. Kernel I/O controls alone cannot establish a drop-in backend.

Trust and coverage

The old separate-atomic runnable gate had a possible lost wakeup and speculative rescheduling. Those exploratory samples are excluded. The corrected code shares its gate with a bounded Loom model (preemption bound 3, up to 10,000 permutations). That model exercises publication/finish races; it does not model a complete actor runtime or prove every possible execution. Independent agy review of the corrected gate and one-reactor I/O found no remaining blockers for that benchmark scope after the correction, while retaining all disclosed prototype limitations.

All measured campaigns retain source revisions, binary hashes, process outcomes, resource limits and raw samples. Default FD failures and blocking watchdogs appear in the report. Initial sandbox-denied socket/measurement runs and smoke-only runs are excluded from measured datasets. Standard workspace tests, runtime-mode contract tests, model checks and lint checks are reported separately from throughput. Public API preservation does not imply every experimental runtime has identical behavior.

Incorporation criteria

A backend is eligible for incorporation only after both performance and compatibility evidence support it. Keep async Tokio as the general-purpose reference. Treat native runnable queues as scheduler prototypes requiring full lifecycle integration. Per-core placement can help locality while worsening skewed-load tails. Spinning consumes CPU even without useful work. The reply experiment is a transport control: the normal async path already uses Tokio oneshots. io_uring results are Linux VM evidence and cannot rank macOS kqueue against Linux kernels directly.

All implementations and tests

The following guide defines every backend/control and test, including semantic differences and future integration work.

Study guide

This study compares runtime ownership, transport costs, scheduling, waiting and I/O. It does not select a production replacement from a single microbenchmark. The public Actor, Handler<M>, protocol, ActorRef, message and reply APIs remain unchanged. Existing defaults remain unchanged. Runtime experiments are compiled only with backend-experiments, selected by a private test environment variable. Native scheduler/transport and I/O controls exist only in bench code.

What each implementation means

Variant Execution resources Purpose and limitations
blocking Persistent actor loops occupy the caller Tokio blocking pool Current Backend::Blocking; the finite pool can be exhausted by a large population of persistent actors.
async Actor futures on the driver's two-worker Tokio runtime Current general-purpose baseline; full Spawned lifecycle and messages.
threads One native OS thread per synchronous actor Current actor implementation; no executor needed by handlers; still uses some Tokio synchronization types.
plain-tokio One task per worker-loop instance on two runtime workers Simpler channel/oneshot control; omits actor cancellation/unwind/type-erasure machinery.
dedicated-default One owner thread plus a default multi-worker Tokio runtime per actor Current Backend::Thread. Resource-heavy at large actor counts. Restricted to small cases in this matrix.
dedicated-one One owner thread plus one runtime worker per actor Reduces runtime worker count, but still has multiple threads per actor.
dedicated-current One owner thread with a current-thread Tokio runtime Removes helper runtime workers. A blocking handler stalls nested helper tasks. Each actor still owns a reactor and descriptors.
dedicated-managed One owner thread per actor, with a process-owned two-worker shared runtime Avoids per-actor reactors and caller-lifetime dependence; helper-resource isolation differs and the pool lives until process exit.
dedicated-shared One owner thread per actor, sharing the caller's two-worker Tokio runtime Avoids per-actor reactors and allows helper progress elsewhere. Caller runtime must outlive actors.
native-block One native thread per prototype actor; bounded addressed mailbox; blocking receive Tokio-free actor/reply data path when bounded replies and direct observation are selected. Does not implement all Spawned lifecycle features.
native-hybrid Native-block plus up to 256 empty polls before blocking Measures the CPU/latency tradeoff of short spinning. It is a fixed policy, not auto-tuned.
native-spin Native-block with continuous empty polling Latency-oriented control; consumes CPU while idle. Limited to four actors to avoid uncontrolled oversubscription.
sharded-1 / sharded-16 Two native workers; actor queues partitioned by actor ID; bounded batches of 1 / 16 Round-robin scans include idle queues. Actor placement is static within each benchmark process.
ready-1 / ready-16 Two native workers share a runnable-actor queue; batches of 1 / 16 Avoids scanning idle actors; shared ready-queue lock can contend. A mutex-protected scheduling gate prevents simultaneous ownership and lost wakeups.
ready-adaptive Shared runnable queue; full/empty-turn-adaptive batch size 1–64, with a 50 µs turn budget Experimental adaptive batching. The time budget is checked between handlers and cannot preempt a handler.
local-ready-16 One runnable queue per worker; fixed actor-to-worker placement; batch 16 Combines active-only scheduling and per-shard placement. Can suffer load imbalance; no work stealing.

Native prototypes use ordinary owned Rust messages and bounded std::sync::mpsc mailboxes (256 slots by default), not Copy-only broadcast rings. A successful send never silently overwrites an unread request. Blocking enqueue can stall a producer when full. They are design controls: dynamic registration, async handler polling, timers, monitors, panic recovery, cancellation and cyclic actor sends still need implementation and tests before such a scheduler can become a backend. They do not establish that a drop-in implementation will have identical speed.

Reply transport experiment

The async-reply-* and threads-reply-* variants deliver the same benchmark-local Probe message through Spawned, carrying an explicitly selected reply transport:

  • std: a general unbounded std::mpsc channel per request.
  • bounded: a one-slot std::mpsc::sync_channel per request.
  • tokio: Tokio's dedicated oneshot primitive per request.

These bypass the normal framework reply envelope to isolate reply choices using a matched message shape. They do not alter public request/reply behavior. Compare within this matched group; comparison with the framework path includes envelope layout and dispatch differences. Allocation counters include driver activity and report successful allocation/reallocation calls and full requested sizes.

All new message experiments use direct reply observation with a process-level watchdog. This avoids a Tokio timeout future per observed reply; thread and future wake mechanisms still differ. The original baseline and its timer-based observer remain available in baseline.rs; historical results are not rewritten.

Scale and workload matrix

Case Actors Producers Measured requests per run Routing / question
rpc1 1 1 32,768 Closed-loop single-request latency.
burst32 1 32 131,072 Finite burst into a busy mailbox; separate collectors.
active128_p32 128 32 131,072 Round-robin traffic reaches every actor.
active128_p128 128 128 131,072 One closed-loop producer per actor.
active512_p128 512 128 262,144 Every actor receives traffic; at most 128 requests in flight.
active1024_p256 1,024 256 262,144 Large population and producer count; resource limits are results.
hotspot128 128 128 131,072 Half of requests go to actor 0; remaining traffic spreads over others. Compare hot and cold p99.
lowload 4 32 10,000 Scheduled 5k requests/s, 5,000 CPU iterations per handler.
overload 4 32 32,768 Scheduled 1M requests/s with the same CPU work.
idle4 4 1 1 One-second idle interval after warmup; reveals spinning CPU cost.
alloc1 1 1 32,768 Allocation counting enabled; not a timing-overhead-free result.

Closed-loop producers wait for replies; increasing the actor population beyond the producer count does not make all actors simultaneously busy. Paced and burst cases can accumulate more outstanding requests. Actor mailboxes may be bounded in prototypes, but collector channels/sample storage remain finite-run driver allocations; no experiment proves safety under indefinite overload.

The original 128-actor baseline had only four active actors. These new scaling cases deliberately send to every actor. Default per-actor multi-worker runtimes are not launched at 512/1024 actors to avoid thousands of runtime threads. One-worker-per-actor is capped at 512. Spin/hybrid controls are capped at four. Skipped combinations are design/resource constraints, not successful measurements.

Runtime compatibility characterization

concurrency/tests/backend_experiments.rs runs each runtime mode in a separate process. It checks:

  1. Nested async spawning and timer completion.
  2. A real TCP request/reply using the runtime's reactor.
  3. Whether a detached helper progresses while the actor blocks.
  4. Actor shutdown and completion.
  5. Actor behavior after its caller runtime is dropped.

Tests intentionally characterize differences: current-thread mode cannot run helpers while a handler blocks, and shared-runtime mode cannot provide independent runtime lifetime. Passing this suite does not mean those variants are drop-in replacements. The standard workspace suite covers ordinary lifecycle behavior; no new default should be chosen without wider client compatibility tests.

Real I/O mechanisms

io_designs.rs reuses persistent loopback TCP connections with TCP_NODELAY. Each connection sends and validates 64-byte request/reply frames. Cases use 1, 16 and 128 connections, 1,000 measured exchanges per connection after warmup. A common native echo server uses one OS thread per connection. The per-connection controls also use one client OS thread per connection. The *-mux controls distribute all connections across one client reactor, and *-mux4 across up to four reactors. The server remains identical across these cases. None is a complete actor backend.

I/O variant Mechanism What it tests
std-io Blocking standard-library TCP Synchronous syscall/socket control.
tokio-io Current-thread Tokio and Mio kqueue on macOS; epoll on Linux.
monoio-legacy Monoio's non-Tokio legacy driver kqueue on macOS; epoll on Linux, with owned-buffer APIs.
monoio-uring Explicit Monoio io_uring driver Linux only; preflight fails explicitly if unavailable or denied. No silent fallback.

Monoio and Tokio differ in buffer ownership, scheduling and code, not just kernel syscalls. Monoio's thread-local futures are not automatically compatible with Spawned's Send handler futures. These tests do not prove that arbitrary existing Tokio-based application handlers can run unchanged on Monoio.

Measurement and reporting

Each sample is a fresh release-mode process, with warmup and randomized ordering. Request IDs and completed counts are checked. Runs retain raw values, failures, compiler/source revisions, environment, descriptor limits and Linux cgroup limits. The watchdog kills the process group, preventing a timed-out child from silently contaminating later samples. Failed samples never receive fabricated throughput.

Handler-completion latency, caller-observed reply latency, queue wait, handler elapsed time and enqueue lag are distinct. CPU and peak RSS are process-wide, including initialization, idle delay, driver/sample storage and teardown. Reported medians of run-level p99s are not pooled p99s. Error bars show run-to-run ranges, not confidence intervals. No cross-OS absolute speed comparison is valid without accounting for the VM and budget differences.

Linux runs in OrbStack's ARM64 VM, with the container restricted to CPUs 0–3, 8 GiB RAM and 4,096 PIDs. Its source is mounted read-only. seccomp=unconfined is used inside this unprivileged VM container to allow io_uring syscalls; this is an experiment setting, not a production security recommendation. Descriptor limits are recorded; a separately raised limit is a distinct experiment. macOS runs use the native host's scheduling and cannot claim equal CPU placement.

Reproduction

python3 benchmarks/design_experiments.py --output /tmp/design-smoke --repetitions 1 --smoke
python3 benchmarks/design_experiments.py --output /tmp/design-mac --repetitions 3
python3 benchmarks/design_experiments.py --output /tmp/design-fd-control --repetitions 3 --group messages --variants dedicated-current --cases active1024_p256 --fd-limit 16384

Use --group, --cases and --variants to limit a campaign. The experimental feature must never be enabled implicitly for production. Public API preservation is a requirement for any eventual backend implementation, not a conclusion from these prototype controls.

Research informing the candidates

  • Seastar's shared-nothing architecture: per-core ownership and explicit cross-core messaging. Our prototype does not reproduce its allocator/network stack.
  • Glommio: cooperative thread-per-core async I/O on Linux io_uring; requires a Linux-specific integration study.
  • Akka dispatcher throughput: bounded mailbox batches trade throughput against fairness.
  • Monoio legacy driver: kqueue/epoll counterpart to its io_uring driver.
  • Mio: OS readiness mechanisms underlying Tokio networking.
  • Compio: portable thread-per-core I/O candidate for later integration; researched, not measured in this campaign.
  • Silver/flux research: transport and observability ideas, with explicit differences from actors.

Scheduler review correction

The first exploratory runnable-queue prototype used separate atomics for a pending count and scheduling flag. Review identified a possible lost notification and spurious rescheduling while a sender had reserved but not published work. Those samples are invalid for selecting a design and are excluded from final graphs.

The measured revision uses support/ready_gate.rs: a mutex serializes producer notification with the worker's lookahead-and-release decision. The worker retains one lookahead message rather than maintaining a speculative pending count. ready_gate_loom.rs models that same gate implementation under publication/finish interleavings. Adaptive batching grows after full turns and resets on empty turns; its clock reads are part of the measured policy cost, not free instrumentation.

Bounded and unbounded burst tails are different admission experiments: blocking a producer delays creation of its next burst timestamp. Burst p99 is therefore not a matched offered-load comparison. Use the absolute-arrival paced cases and a separately pre-sized capacity control before attributing differences to queue implementation. Hotspot placement deliberately creates a hot shard; it measures load imbalance as well as batching. Worker counts and total process CPU budgets are distinct controls.

Multiplexed I/O variants (tokio-mux, monoio-legacy-mux, monoio-uring-mux) drive all connections on one client runtime/thread. The per-connection-runtime variants remain as resource controls. They use the same native echo server; server thread costs remain common confounders. Linux io_uring is explicitly selected and preflighted, with no silent fallback.

Additional controls include the existing Backend::Blocking pool, and I/O multiplexing on four client reactors (*-mux4) as well as one (*-mux). Per-reactor connections are partitioned round-robin; both configurations use the same echo server. This separates reactor amortization from a one-client-core bottleneck. Blocking-pool exhaustion is captured by a shorter process watchdog in its separate capacity study, rather than fabricated as zero throughput.
